The Slaty robin (Peneothello cyanus) is a passerine endemic to the montane forests of New Guinea, where it occupies the understory of Nothofagus-dominated stands. Field studies on the species' reproductive biology have documented that eggs are laid in a cup-shaped nest constructed of moss and rootlets, typically placed in a tree fork one to three meters above the ground. Based on measurements of a single clutch, the egg length averages 23.5 millimeters and the egg width averages 18 millimeters, from which a volume-based calculation yields a hatchling mass of 4.0 grams [Wwb = 4.0 grams]. This modest neonatal mass reflects the altricial state of the young, which are entirely dependent on parental provisioning during the early nestling period. Incubation at a nest temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C] lasts approximately 12 days [ab = approximately 12 days] before hatching occurs, a developmental duration that is consistent with values reported for other small-bodied Australasian robins of similar adult mass. The thermal regime maintained by the incubating adult appears critical for synchronizing embryonic development within this narrow altricial window.

Once the eggs have hatched, the altricial nestlings progress through a series of developmental milestones under the sustained metabolic support provided by both parents. Fledging, marked by the achievement of sustained flight, occurs at 12.5 days since birth [tx = 12.5 days since birth], a brief nestling period sustained by the parents' metabolic capacity at a body temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This relatively brief nestling period is characteristic of many montane tropical passerines, which must accelerate growth to reduce predation risk during the vulnerable brooding phase. The fledging event is marked by the achievement of first flight and subsequent nest departure, after which the young remain dependent on adult feeding for an extended period as they develop foraging proficiency. The early nutritional independence phase is thus preceded by a highly condensed period of somatic growth and feather maturation, all sustained by the high metabolic throughput of the adults. The energetic costs associated with this provisioning effort are considerable and are closely linked to the basal metabolic demands of the provisioning birds.

The basal oxygen consumption of adult Slaty robins has been measured under controlled laboratory conditions, providing insights into the energetic underpinnings of their life history. At a thermoneutral ambient temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], which corresponds closely to the species' active body temperature, the resting metabolic rate was recorded at 63 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 63 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This value, when standardized to body mass, is consistent with the allometric expectations for a passerine of this size inhabiting a cool montane environment, where relatively high metabolic rates are often necessary to maintain homeothermy. The measurement was obtained from post-absorptive adults during the inactive phase of their circadian cycle, ensuring that the recorded oxygen consumption reflected true basal conditions. Such physiological data are essential for constructing energy budgets and for understanding how the species allocates resources between self-maintenance and reproductive effort across its annual cycle. The high metabolic cost of thermoregulation in the cool cloud-forest habitat likely imposes strong selective pressure on behavioral strategies such as huddling during brooding.

The species exhibits pronounced sexual size dimorphism in ultimate adult body mass, a trait that may influence several aspects of its ecology and behavior. Based on specimens collected from across its elevational range, adult females achieve an ultimate wet weight of 23.275 grams [Wwi = 23.275 grams], whereas adult males attain a larger ultimate wet weight of 26 grams [Wwi = 26 grams]. This difference likely reflects the energetic demands of egg production in females and the role of male body size in territory defense, as the species is known to maintain year-round territories in the understory. The larger mass of males may confer an advantage in agonistic interactions with conspecifics, particularly during the establishment of breeding territories that contain suitable nest sites. The dimorphism is evident even in subadult birds, suggesting that sex-specific growth trajectories diverge early during the post-fledging period. The ecological significance of this mass difference is further underscored by its constancy across high-elevation populations, indicating a canalized developmental pathway.

Reproductive output in the Slaty robin is characterized by a relatively slow pace compared to many temperate passerines, a pattern common among tropical montane species. Under the thermal conditions typical of the species' active state (40 °C [T = 40 °C]), the maximum reported lifespan is 9.1 years [am = 9.1 years], a longevity that is considerable for a bird of this body mass. Puberty is attained relatively late, with sexual maturity occurring at 37.5 days since birth [tp = 37.5 days since birth], though first successful reproduction is typically deferred until 1.4 years since birth [tR = 1.4 years since birth] as young birds establish territories and acquire sufficient experience at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C] at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This low annual reproductive rate is compensated by an extended lifespan and high adult survival. Females typically produce a clutch of two eggs [N_R_i = a clutch of two eggs] and field observations suggest that they raise one brood per year [F_R_i = one brood per year] due to the constrained length of the favorable breeding season at high elevations. This life-history strategy, combining delayed reproduction, low fecundity, and extended longevity, is consistent with a slow-paced life history shaped by the stable but resource-limited conditions of the montane forest environment.
